column2: Having reached the other shore, one does not resolve to cross again; its fall in the great ocean is seen to be hard to find.
As a boat laden and tied by a rope on the great waters, so the body drags by application of the mind.
As other rivers are stitched together around the ocean, so nature is ever stitched together by yoga.
Men with minds clinging to snares of affection of many kinds, abiding in nature, sink like a house of sand in water.
For the embodied one who stays in the house of the body, whose holy place is purity, and who has set out on the path of intellect, there is happiness here and hereafter.
Expansions are joined with affliction, but brief statements bring happiness; all expansions are for others; they know renunciation as the good of the self.
The circle of friends born of intention, kinsmen with a cause, wife, servants and sons all engage for their own ends.
Neither mother nor father gets anything for anyone; a creature with the rice of giving as wholesome food enjoys the fruit of his own deeds.
Mother, son, father, brother, wife and friends are set like a die in the place of a step on a chessboard.
All deeds done before, good and bad, go with a creature; knowing the fruit of action at hand, the inner self urges the intellect accordingly.
He who goes forth with resolve and finds helpers: for him no undertaking ever sinks.
Fortune never abandons the brave, steadfast, wise man of single mind, joined, as rays never leave the sun.
The man of blameless self who begins anything with faith and resolve, by right means and wonder, with intellect, finds no purpose failing.

A creature of itself meets the good and bad deeds that all fixed to it; from the womb it gains both what it did before; death is inescapable, equal in course, cut off by time; like flour ground by a stone, it brings the work to its end.
His own form, the extent of his making, family descent, accumulation of wealth: every man gains as he has done, by good or bad action made by himself.
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed truly by the wise, Janaka, king, best of the knowers of dharma, heard it and reached supreme joy.
[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you an ancient tale, the dialogue of the Sadhyas with the Swan, Yudhishthira.
Becoming a golden swan, the unborn, eternal Prajapati roams the three worlds, and then approached the Sadhyas.
[The Sadhyas said:] 'Bird, we are the gods called Sadhyas; we ask you, for you are said to know liberation: we ask the dharma of liberation.
We have heard you are wise and a speaker of the steadfast; a good word falls from you, bird: what do you hold the best, twice-born, and in what does your mind, great soul, delight?
Instruct us, best of birds, in the one task you hold best among tasks, by doing which a man is quickly freed from all bonds, lord of birds.'

[The Swan said:] 'I hear this is the task, you who eat nectar: austerity, self-control, truth, guarding the self; loosening all the knots of the heart, one should bring the dear and undear under one's power.
He should not be a wounder of others, nor speak cruelly, nor take the highest from the lowly; with whatever speech another is alarmed, he should not speak that harsh, sinful speech.
Arrows of speech go out from the mouth, struck by which one grieves day and night; they fall on the vital parts of another; the wise man should not let them go on others.

The force of speech, the force of mind, the force of anger, the force of contentiousness, the force of belly and genitals: the one who bears these forces when they rise, I think a brahmana and a sage.
The unangry is better than the angry; the patient better than the impatient; the human better than the non-human; the knowing better than the ignorant is chief.
Abused, one should not abuse; the anger of the patient burns the abuser and he gains his good deeds.
He who, when addressed harshly, does not speak rough or dear words, and, struck, does not strike back from steadiness, nor wishes ill for his striker: the gods always long for him.
One should be patient with a worse, a better and an equal; slighted, struck and abused thus he will reach success.
I ever serve the noble, humble as I am; I have no contentiousness and no anger; nor do I go seeking gain, nor do I go by any crookedness.
Cursed, I do not curse back; I know self-control as the door to the immortal here; this secret Brahman I tell you: there is nothing higher than man.
Freed from sins, like the moon from clouds, free of dust, awaiting time, the steadfast one succeeds by steadiness.
He who is worthy of honour by all, like a post in a sprinkling, well born, of whom good speech is said: that self-controlled one goes to the gods.
They do not wish to speak of the virtues of a man as they wish to speak of his lack of virtues, those who inquire after them.
He whose speech and mind are always rightly set gains all this, the Vedas, austerity and renunciation.
The wise grows by the abuse and dishonour of the unwise; therefore one should not exalt another nor despise oneself.
The twice-born should be satisfied with dishonour as with nectar; the dishonoured sleeps happily, but he who dishonours perishes.
What the angry man sacrifices, what he gives, the austerity he practises, what he offers: Vaivasvata takes it all of his; the angry man's toil is in vain.
He who has four doors well guarded, best of the immortals: the genital, belly, hands and speech as fourth, he knows dharma.
Practising truth, self-control, honesty, non-cruelty, steadiness and patience, ever devoted to study, coveting nothing of others, delighting in solitude, he would go upward.
Following all these as a calf follows four teats, I have found nothing anywhere more purifying than truth.
I say to men, moving among the gods: truth is the stairway to heaven, like a boat to the far shore of the sea.
As a man lives with such, as he serves such, and as he wishes to be, such he becomes.
Whether one serves the good or the bad, an ascetic or a thief, as a garment takes the colour it is dyed, so he comes under their power.
The gods always converse with the good; they do not go to see a human object; not even the moon is equal; for the wind is unequal, who knows high and low objects.
When a man is of blameless heart, the gods are pleased by him who stands in the path of the good.
Those who are always devoted to the organ and belly, thieves and always harsh in speech: the gods, knowing them to be full of faults, avoid them from afar.
The gods are not to be pleased by a man of low goodness, an all-eater or doer of bad deeds; those true to truth, grateful, devoted to dharma, they meet with.
The unspoken is better than the spoken, they say; one should speak truth, which is second to the unspoken; one should speak dharma, the third; one should speak the pleasant, the fourth.'
[The Sadhyas said:] 'By what is the world covered, by what does it not shine? By what does one give up friends, and by what does one not go to heaven?'
[The Swan said:] 'The world is covered by ignorance; from envy it does not shine; from greed one gives up friends; from attachment one does not go to heaven.'
[The Sadhyas said:] 'Who alone delights among brahmanas? Who alone sits in silence with many? Who alone is strong, though weak? Who of these does not enter into quarrel?'
[The Swan said:] 'The wise one alone delights among brahmanas; the wise one alone sits in silence with many; the wise one alone is strong though weak; the wise one does not enter into quarrel.'
[The Sadhyas said:] 'What is the godhood of brahmanas, what is their goodness said to be, what their badness, what their humanness?'
[The Swan said:] 'Study is their godhood, vow is said to be their goodness, slander their badness, and death their humanness.'
[Bhishma said:] This dialogue of the Sadhyas is called supreme; the field of actions, the womb, goodness, is called truth."
[Bhishma said:] "The Sankhyas praise Sankhya, and the yogis, the twice-born, praise yoga; they say by reasons that their own is better, to establish their side.
How can one without a lord be freed? so, scourge of foes, the yogis, the wise rightly say, by reasons, that theirs is better.
The Sankhyas, the twice-born, rightly say this reason: having known all the courses here, whoever is detached from objects
will plainly be freed above the body, not otherwise; the greatly wise say this: Sankhya is the vision of liberation.
The reason in one's own side is to be taken, as capable, beneficial speech; the view of the refined is to be accepted by those like you who are esteemed by the refined.
Yoga has perceptible reasons, Sankhya has settled determinations in scripture; both of these are my view of the truth, dear Yudhishthira.
Both of these, king, are views of knowledge accepted by the refined; practised according to the shastra, they lead to the highest goal.
Purity is equal for both, and compassion to beings, sinless one; keeping vows is equal; the view is not equal.
As the large unwinking fish break the net and again reach the water, so yogis, freed from stain, reach that state.
So also as strong deer, breaking the snare, reach a clear path freed from all bonds,
so, king, the strong yogis, cutting the bonds born of greed, go to the supreme, stainless, auspicious path.
But weak deer in the snares perish, without doubt; so do those without yogic strength.
And the weak, Kaunteya, as fish caught in a net, come to their end, king of kings; so are the weak yogis.
As small birds, reaching a fine net, are clinging and perish there, but the strong are freed,
so, scourge of foes, yogis bound by bonds of action: the weak perish, the strong are freed.
As a small fire, king, dies down when weak, overwhelmed by thick fuel, so yoga is weak, lord.
And when that same fire has gained strength, king, joined with wind, it would quickly burn the whole earth.
So a yogi who has gained strength, blazing with energy, of great power, like the sun at the end of time, would dry up the whole world.
As a weak man is carried off by a current, king, so weak yoga is carried off helplessly by objects.
And as the lord of waters checks that same current, so having gained the strength of yoga one disposes many objects.
Yogis endowed with the strength of yoga, Partha, enter helpless Prajapatis, sages, gods and great elements, being lords.
Neither Yama, nor the ender, nor angry Death of dreadful valour rules over any of those of immeasurable splendour in yoga, king.
Yoga, having gained strength, can make many thousands of selves, bull of the Bharatas, and with all of them roam the earth.
He could gain objects and again perform fierce austerity, and draw them in again, Partha, as the sun draws in the qualities of its energy.
For yoga that stands in strength, lord of bondage, king, power over liberation is surely attained.
These strengths in yoga have been told by me, lord of the people; I shall again tell you subtle things for illustration.
Regarding concentration of the self and the practice of holding, lord, hear from me subtle illustrations, bull of the Bharatas.
As an archer, careful and collected, hits his target, so the yogi, rightly joined, reaches liberation, without doubt.
As a man climbs a ladder carrying a vessel full of oil with his mind set unmoving, with the mind joined and striving,
so, king, yoga, joining the self unmoving, makes the self stainless, with a vision like the sun.
As a helmsman, Kaunteya, collected, would quickly bring a boat on the great ocean to a port, king,
so the knower of truth, having joined the self in concentration by yoga, reaches the hard-to-reach place, leaving this body, king.
And as a charioteer, careful, having yoked good horses, quickly brings the archer to the desired place, bull among men,
so, king, the yogi collected in his holdings quickly reaches the supreme place, as a freed arrow the target.
The yogi who stands unmoving, having placed the self in the self, destroys sin and gains the ageless state, like a hunter of fish.
At the navel, the throat, the head, the heart, the chest, the sides, in seeing, touching and in the nose, of immeasurable valour,
the yogi who in these places, collected in the great vow, joins the subtle self by the self, rightly, lord of the people,
quickly, with stainless wisdom, burning up the deed good and bad, resorting to the highest yoga, is freed if he wishes."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Having made what foods and having conquered what, Bharata, does the yogi gain strength? You should tell this."
[Bhishma said:] "Intent on eating grains and oil-cake, and on avoiding oils, the yogi would gain strength.
Eating dry barley for a long time, scourge of foes, delighting in solitude, pure of self, the yogi would gain strength.
Moving through fortnights, months and varied seasons and in caves, drinking water mixed with milk, the yogi would gain strength.
Or fasting a whole month unbroken, constantly, lord of men, rightly, pure of self, the yogi would gain strength.
Having conquered desire and anger, cold and heat, rain, fear, sleep, breath, manliness and objects,
and the hard-to-conquer discontent, and dreadful craving, king, and all touches, and the hard-to-conquer drowsiness, best of kings,
great souls, free of attachment, greatly wise, kindle the subtle self by the self by the wealth of meditation and study.
This path of the wise brahmanas is held hard to travel; no one, bull of the Bharatas, goes on it in safety.
As a young man might fall into a dreadful forest with many snakes and reptiles, waterless like a pit, hard to pass, full of thorns,
without food, mostly forest, with trees burnt by wildfire, a path full of robbers, and come out in safety,
so a twice-born who follows the path of yoga, ceasing in safety, is held to have many faults from the path.
It is easier to stand on the sharp edge of a razor, lord of the earth, than for the unself-controlled to stand in the holdings of yoga.
Holdings that have failed, dear, do not lead to a good goal, like boats without helmsmen carrying men on the sea, king.
But he who, Kaunteya, stands in the holdings by rule is freed from death, birth, sorrow and pleasure.
This has been told, set forth in many shastras, in the yogas; the supreme yoga, whole, is settled among the twice-born.
That is the great supreme Brahman of the great soul: Brahma, the lord, the giver of boons, Vishnu, Bhava, Dharma and the six-faced one, and the great-natured sons of Brahma.
Darkness, passion, and the pure goodness; supreme nature; success; the goddess, the wife of Varuna; all energy and great steadiness.
The pure ruler of men; the Vishvadevas, serpents and ancestors; all mountains and dreadful oceans; all rivers and thundering clouds;
nagas, mountains, hosts of yakshas, directions, gandharvas, men and women: reaching each other, the great soul, the yogi, would enter and soon be freed.
And this tale that is attached to the god of great valour and wisdom, auspicious, the one who overcomes all mortals by yogas, the great soul whose self is Narayana, does."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Now tell me the rule of Sankhya in full, as I ask; for you know all knowledge in the three worlds."
[Bhishma said:] "Hear from me this pure doctrine of the Sankhyas who know the self, ordained by awakened ascetics and lords such as Kapila,
in which, bull among men, no confusions are seen, and many virtues, and only the removal of faults.
Having reckoned by knowledge the objects with their faults, king, human ones, hard to conquer, all, and the objects of the pishachas,
having known the objects of rakshasas and of yakshas, the objects of serpents and of gandharvas,
having known the objects of ancestors, of those who move among animals, king, the objects of Suparna and of the Maruts,
having known the objects of royal sages and of Brahmarshis, the objects of the asuras and of the Vishvedevas,
having known the objects of divine sages and the lords of yogas, the objects of the lords of creatures and of Brahma,
and the sorrow, when the time comes, of those who fall seeking objects, the sorrow of those who fall among animals and of those who fall in hell,
all the virtues of heaven and all faults, Bharata, the faults in Vedic disputation and the Vedic virtues,
the faults in the yoga of knowledge and the virtues in yoga, king, the faults in Sankhya knowledge and likewise its virtues,
having known sattva as tenfold, rajas as ninefold, tamas as eightfold, and intellect as sevenfold,
having known space with its quality, the mind as fivefold, intellect as fourfold, and the great tamas as threefold,
having known rajas as twofold and sattva again as one, having known the path in truth and the observation at dissolution,
those endowed with knowledge and discernment, formed by auspicious causes, gain auspicious liberation, subtle, here beyond space.
The eye is joined to form, the nose to the quality of smell, the ear attached to sound, the tongue to the qualities of taste,
the body attached to touch, wind resting in space, delusion clinging to tamas, greed resting on objects,
Vishnu in the stride, Shakra in strength, fire clinging in the belly, the goddess in the waters; the waters rest in light.
Light clings to wind, wind rests in space, space is joined to the great, and the great rests in intellect;
intellect clings to tamas, tamas rests in rajas, rajas clings to sattva, and sattva clings to the self;
the self clings to the lord, the god Narayana; the god clings to liberation, and liberation clings to nothing.
Knowing the body joined with sattva, covered with sixteen qualities, knowing nature and consciousness resting in the body,
the one self standing in the middle, in whom sin is not found, knowing the second, action, among kings who seek objects,
the senses and the objects of the senses, all dissolved in the self, and prana, apana, samana, vyana and udana in truth,
knowing the downward wind and the flowing wind, and the seven winds and the rest, sevenfold by rule again,
the Prajapatis and sages and the many excellent paths, scourge of foes, knowing the many seven sages and royal sages,
the divine sages and other great sages like the sun, knowing them fallen from lordship after a great time, king,
hearing of the destruction of great hosts of beings, lord of the earth, and knowing the inauspicious goal of sinful doers, king,
and the sorrow of those fallen in the Vaitarani in Yama's abode, and the inauspicious wanderings in varied wombs,
dwelling in the inauspicious womb, a vessel of blood and water, with phlegm, urine and excrement and a strong stench,
in an aggregate of semen and blood, grasped by marrow and sinew, in an impure city of nine gates, crowded with hundreds of veins,
knowing the self as harmed, and the manifold yogas, king, and the lovely enclosure of tamasic creatures,
and the despised state of the sattvic creatures, Bharata, blamed for the sake of the great, and the Sankhyas who know the self,
the dreadful disasters of the moon and the sun, seeing the fall of stars and the turning of constellations,
knowing the wretched separation of pairs, king, and seeing the mutual devouring of beings, and their inauspiciousness,
knowing delusion in childhood and the inauspicious decay of the body, with sattva resting somewhere when passion and delusion arrive,
among thousands some man resorts to the thought of liberation, knowing, from hearing first, the rarity of liberation,
great regard for what is not gained, then indifference to what is gained, and again knowing, king, the wickedness of objects,
and seeing the inauspicious bodies of the lifeless, Kaunteya, and knowing the sorrow of dwelling in families, Bharata,
knowing the dreadful goal of the killers of brahmanas, of the fallen, of the evil-souled brahmanas addicted to drink, and the bad goal of those attached to the teacher's wife,
those, Yudhishthira, who do not behave rightly toward their mothers, and men who do not live properly in worlds with gods,
knowing by that knowledge the goal of the doers of evil, and knowing separately the courses of those born in animal wombs,
the varied Vedic discussions, the turning of seasons, the waning of years, the waning of months,
seeing the waning of fortnights, the waning of days, and seeing directly the waning and waxing of the moon,
seeing the rise of oceans and their fall again, the loss of wealth and its growth again,
seeing the decline of enjoyments and especially of the ages, seeing the decline of mountains and rivers,
seeing the decay of classes and the end of decay again and again, seeing old age, death and birth, and sorrows,
knowing the faults of the body and, in truth, their sorrow, and rightly knowing the helplessness of the gods, Bharata,
knowing the faults of the self, all resting in the self, and knowing the bad smells arisen from one's own body,
[Yudhishthira said:] "What faults born of your own body do you see, of immeasurable valour? You should tell me all this doubt truly."
[Bhishma said:] "Lord, the wise, the Kapila Sankhyas who know the way, speak of five faults in the body; hear them, scourge of foes.
Desire, anger, fear, sleep, and breath as fifth: these faults are seen in bodies of all embodied beings.
They cut anger by forbearance, desire by giving up intentions, sleep by cultivating goodness, fear by heedfulness, and the fifth, breath, by light diet, king.
Knowing virtues by hundreds of virtues, faults by hundreds of faults, causes by hundreds of varied causes, knowing the varied in truth,
the world like foam of water, covered with hundreds of Vishnu's illusions, like a painted wall of the mind, a reed without essence, useless,
seeing darkness like a pit, like a bubble in the rain, mostly of destruction, devoid of pleasure, ending in non-being; rajas sunk in tamas like an elephant helpless in mud;
the Sankhyas, king, greatly wise, give up the body made by the subjects, by Sankhya which is to be known by knowledge, pervading and great, king,
cutting quickly with the sword of knowledge, with the rod of austerity, Bharata, the bad smells of rajas, and those of tamas, and the holy smells of sattva, born of touch and resting in the body.
Then the dreadful waters of sorrow, the great lake of worry and grief, with disease and death as great crocodiles, the great serpent of great fear,
with tamas as tortoise and rajas as fish, they cross by wisdom; with the mud of affection and old age as stronghold, and touch as islands, scourge of foes,
with action as its depth, truth its shore, steadfast vow, this one, king; violence its swift great current, and the great mine of manifold tastes,
with various delights as great jewels, with sorrow and fever as winds, grief and craving as great whirlpools, sharp disease as great elephants,
the collection of aggregates of bones, with phlegm as foam, scourge of foes, giving as the pearl mine, terrible, with the lake of blood flowing,
with a roar of laughter and shouting, hard to cross by manifold knowledge, with the dirt and alkali of weeping and tears, with renunciation of attachment as its refuge,
the flood of the world of rebirth, the city of sons and kinsmen, with non-violence and truth as limits, with the great waves of giving up life,
with the Vedanta as its island and compassion for all beings as its sea, an ocean with the mouth of the undersea fire, whose object is hard to reach by liberation,
the sages and perfected ones cross it by the yoga of knowledge, Bharata, and having crossed the hard-to-cross birth they enter the stainless sky.
Then the sun carries those virtuous Sankhyas with his rays, entering them like lotus-fibres, carrying them across objects, king.
There the Pravaha wind receives them, Bharata: the detached ascetics, the perfected, the strong, rich in austerity.
Subtle, cool, fragrant and pleasant to touch, Bharata, the best of the seven winds goes to the holy worlds; he carries them, Kaunteya, to the supreme goal beyond space.
Space carries, lord of the world, to the highest goal of rajas; rajas carries, king of kings, to the highest goal of sattva.
Sattva carries the pure-souled to the supreme Narayana, the lord; the lord, pure-souled, carries by the self to the Supreme Self.
Having reached the Supreme Self, stainless in the seat of beings, they become fit for immortality and do not return, lord; that is the supreme goal, Partha, of the great souls beyond the pairs."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Having reached the highest place, the blessed one, the steadfast in vow, do they remember it until birth and death, sinless one, or not?
What is true in this, you should tell me as it is; apart from you, Kauravya, I have no other man to ask.
This is a great fault of liberation: if sages who have gone, having attained success, remain in that same knowledge, they are supreme ascetics.
I see the dharma marked by activity as supreme, king; for one sunk in the supreme knowledge, what could be sorrier?"

[Bhishma said:] "Your question, dear, has been asked with great difficulty, properly; even the awakened are bewildered by this question, bull of the Bharatas. Here too hear the supreme truth, rightly told by fear.
Where the supreme intellect of the great-souled Kapilas is, the senses too know their own body of the embodied, king; for the sake of the self they are; the subtle one sees by them.
Deprived of the self, they are like logs and stumps and perish, without doubt, like foam on the great ocean.
Scourge of enemies, the subtle one of the embodied who sleeps with the senses roams everywhere, like the wind in the sky.
He sees properly and touches touches, lord, understanding all as before, Bharata.
All the senses here, each in its place by rule, dissolve for want of mastery, like serpents with poison struck.
But the self moves subtle everywhere, entering the places of all the senses; there is no doubt.
All the qualities of sattva, and again the qualities of rajas, and all the qualities of tamas, and the qualities of intellect, Bharata..."
Then those brahmanas, rising at dawn, reported to the king what had been said by Agni, all amazed.
Choose me, good luck to you, or choose the king Marutta; or leaving Marutta, serve me as you please.
Seeing him sitting so, motionless, the king of the Kurus, Kaunteya, slayer of heroes, hurried in distress.
I have seen this slaughter of the Yadavas, and before it of the kings and the chiefs of the Kurus; I am not able today to see this city of the Yadavas without the Yadus.
This is the holy divine river, Partha, purifier of the three worlds, the Ganga of the sky, king of kings; bathe there and you will go.
